en.content: The general solution of the differential equation $$\left(3 x y+y^2\right) d x+\left(x^2+x y\right) d y=0$$ is

$$\begin{aligned} & \left(3 x y+y^2\right) d x+\left(x^2+x y\right) d y=0 \\ & \therefore \frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{\left(3 x y+y^2\right)}{\left(x^2+x y\right)} \end{aligned}$$

Put $$y=v x \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=v+x \frac{d v}{d x}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore v+x \frac{d v}{d x}=-\frac{\left(3 v x^2+v^2 x^2\right)}{\left(x^2+v^2\right)}=-\frac{3 v+v^2}{1+v} \\ & \therefore x \frac{d v}{d x}=-\frac{3 v+v^2}{1+v}-v=-\frac{\left(2 v^2+4 v\right)}{1+v} \\ & \therefore \int \frac{1+v}{\left(2 v^2+4 v\right)} d v=\int \frac{-1}{x} d x \\ & \therefore \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{v+1}{v^2+2 v} d v=-\int \frac{d x}{x} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{4} \int \frac{2(v+1)}{v^2+2 v} d v=-\log x+\log c_1 \\ & \therefore \frac{1}{4} \log \left(v^2+2 v\right)+\log x=\log c_1 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{4} \log \left(\frac{y^2}{x^2}+\frac{2 y}{x}\right)+\log x=\log c_1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{1}{4} \log \left(\frac{y^2+2 x y}{x^2}\right)+\log x=\log c_1 \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{y^2+2 x y}{x^2}\right)+\log x^4=4 \log c_1 \\ & \therefore \log \left[\left(\frac{y^2+2 x y}{x^2}\right)\left(x^4\right)\right]=\log c_1^4 \Rightarrow \log \left[x^2\left(y^2+2 x y\right)\right]=\log c_1^4 \\ & \therefore x^2\left(y^2+2 x y\right)=c \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Negation of the statement $$\forall x \in R, x^2+1=0$$ is
en.explanation:
To find the negation of the given statement, we start by understanding the original statement:

$$\forall x \in R, x^2+1=0$$

This statement declares that for every real number \(x\), the equation \(x^2+1=0\) holds true. The negation of a statement changes its truth value, essentially turning a universally quantified statement (one that applies to all members of a set) into an existentially quantified statement (one that applies to at least one member of the set), and vice versa. Additionally, it inverts the condition within the statement.

To negate the given statement, we apply the following steps:

  • Change the universal quantifier (\(\forall\)) to an existential quantifier (\(\exists\)).
  • Invert the condition \(x^2+1=0\) to \(x^2+1 \neq 0\). The condition \(x^2+1=0\) being true for all \(x\) in \(R\) is the original claim, so negation requires that there's at least one \(x\) in \(R\) for which that condition doesn't hold.

Therefore, the negation is: "There exists at least one real number \(x\) for which \(x^2+1 \neq 0\)."

This means Option B is the correct negation:

$$\exists x \in R$$ such that $$x^2+1 \neq 0$$.

Options A and C introduce inequalities that were not part of the original statement and thus are incorrect. Option D repeats the original statement, which is not a negation.

en.content: A body at an unknown temperature is placed in a room which is held at a constant temperature of $$30^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$$. If after 10 minutes the temperature of the body is $$0^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$$ and after 20 minutes the temperature of the body is $$15^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$$, then the expression for the temperature of the body at any time $$\mathrm{t}$$ is
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} & \text { We have } \frac{\mathrm{dT}}{\mathrm{dt}} \propto(30-\mathrm{T}) \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{dT}}{\mathrm{dt}}=-\mathrm{K}(30-\mathrm{T}) \Rightarrow \int \frac{\mathrm{dT}}{30-\mathrm{T}}=\int-\mathrm{Kt} \\ & \therefore \log |30-\mathrm{T}|=-\mathrm{kt}+\mathrm{c} \quad \text{.....(1)} \end{aligned}$$

From given data, we write

$$\log |30-0|=-10 \mathrm{~K}+\mathrm{c}$$ ..... (2)

$$\log |30-0|=-20 \mathrm{~K}+\mathrm{c}$$ ..... (3)

Solving (2) and (3), we get

$$\log \left(\frac{30}{15}\right)=10 \mathrm{~K} \Rightarrow \mathrm{K}=\frac{1}{10} \log 2$$

Substituting value of $$K$$ in eq. (2), we get

$$\log 30=(-10)\left(\frac{\log 2}{10}\right)+c \Rightarrow c=\log 60$$

Thus eq. (1) becomes

$$\begin{aligned} & \log |30-\mathrm{T}|=\frac{-\log 2}{10} \mathrm{t}+\log 60 \\ & \therefore \log \left|\frac{30-\mathrm{T}}{60}\right|=\frac{-0.3010}{10} \mathrm{t}=-0.03010 \mathrm{t} \\ & \therefore \frac{30-\mathrm{T}}{60}=\mathrm{e}^{-0.03010 \mathrm{t}} \quad \therefore \mathrm{T}=-60 \mathrm{e}^{-0.03010 \mathrm{t}}+30 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: $$\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x-1}{x-2}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x+1}{x+2}\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}$$, then the values of $$x$$ are

en.content: A stone is thrown into a quite lake and the waves formed move in circles. If the radius of a circular wave increases at the rate of 4 cm/sec, then the rate of increase in its area, at the instant when its radius is 10 cm, is _________ cm$$^2$$/sec.

en.content: The function $$f(x)=\cot ^{-1} x+x$$ is increasing in the interval.

en.content: $$\lim _\limits{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{(2 x-3)(\sqrt{x}-1)}{2 x^2+x-3}=$$
en.explanation: $$\begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{(2 x-3)(\sqrt{x}-1)}{2 x^2+x-3} \\ = & \lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{(2 x-3)(\sqrt{x}-1)}{(x-1)(2 x+3)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{(2 x-3)(\sqrt{x}-1)}{(\sqrt{x}-1)(\sqrt{x}+1)(2 x+3)} \\ = & \lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{2 x-3}{(\sqrt{x}+1)(2 x+3)}=\frac{-1}{2(5)}=\frac{-1}{10}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: The product of the perpendicular distances from $$(2,-1)$$ to the pair of lines $$2 x^2-5 x y+2 y^2=0$$ is
en.explanation:
$$2 x^2-5 x y+2 y^2=0$$

$$\therefore 2 x^2-4 x y-x y+2 y^2=0 \Rightarrow 2 x(x-2 y)-y(x-2 y)=0$$

$$\therefore(2 \mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y})(\mathrm{x}-2 \mathrm{y})=0 \quad$$ Thus lines are $$2 \mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y}=0$$ and $$\mathrm{x}-2 \mathrm{y}=0$$

Distance of point $$(2,-1)$$ from these two lines are respectively $$\left|\frac{(2)(2)+(-1)(-1)}{\sqrt{4+1}}\right|$$ and $$\left|\frac{(1)(2)+(-1)(-2)}{\sqrt{1+4}}\right|$$ i.e. $$\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}}$$ and $$\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}$$

Hence required answer is $$\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \times \frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}=4$$

en.content: For two data sets each of size 5 , the variance are given to be 4 and 5 and the corresponding means are given to be 2 and 4 respectively. The variance of the combined data set is

en.content: The curves $$\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1$$ and $$y^3=16 x$$ intersect each other orthogonally, then $$a^2=$$
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1 \\ & \therefore \frac{1}{a^2} 2 x+\frac{1}{4} 2 y \frac{d y}{d x}=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d x}=\left(\frac{-x}{a^2}\right)\left(\frac{4}{y}\right) \quad \text{.....(1)}\\ \end{aligned}$$

Also $$\mathrm{y}^3=16 \mathrm{x}$$

$$\therefore 3 y^2 \frac{d y}{d x}=16 \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{16}{3 y^2}$$ ...... (2)

Since curves intersect orthogonally, from (1) and (2), we write

$$\begin{aligned} & \left(\frac{-x}{a^2}\right)\left(\frac{4}{y}\right)\left(\frac{16}{3 y^2}\right)=-1 \\ & \therefore \frac{64 x}{3 a^2 y^3}=1 \text { and we have } y^3=16 x \\ & \therefore \frac{64 x}{3 a^2(16 x)}=1 \Rightarrow a^2=\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The molar specific heats of an ideal gas at constant pressure and volume are denoted by '$$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{p}}$$' and '$$C_v$$' respectively. If $$\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}$$ and '$$R$$' is universal gas constant, then $$C_v$$ is equal to

en.content: In a pure silicon, number of electrons and holes per unit volume are $$1.6 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$$. If silicon is doped with Boron in a way that on doping hole density increases to $$4 \times 10^{22} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$$. Then electron density in doped semiconductor will be

en.content: A monoatomic gas at pressure '$$\mathrm{P}$$' having volume '$$\mathrm{V}$$' expands isothermally to a volume $$2 \mathrm{~V}$$ and then adiabatically to a volume $$16 \mathrm{~V}$$. The final pressure of the gas is $$\left(\gamma=\frac{5}{3}\right)$$

For adiabatic process : $$\quad \mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2^\gamma=\mathrm{P}_3 \mathrm{~V}_3^\gamma$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad P_3 & =P_2\left(\frac{V_2}{V_3}\right)^\gamma=P_2\left(\frac{2 V_1}{V_3}\right)^\gamma=\frac{P_1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{5 / 3} \quad\left[\because \frac{V_1}{V_3}=\frac{1}{16}\right] \\ & =\frac{P_1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{32}=\frac{P_1}{64} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A particle moves in a circular orbit of radius '$$r$$' under a central attractive force, $$F=-\frac{k}{r}$$, where $$\mathrm{k}$$ is a constant. The periodic time of its motion is proportional to
en.explanation: $$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{mr} \omega^2=\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{r}} \\ & \therefore \omega^2=\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{mr}^2} \quad \therefore \omega^2 \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}^2} \\ & \therefore \quad \omega \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}}, \mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega} \quad \therefore \mathrm{T} \propto \mathrm{r}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: A black reactangular surface of area '$$a$$' emits energy '$$\mathrm{E}$$' per second at $$27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$. If length and breadth is reduced to $$\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\text {rd }}$$ of initial value and temperature is raised to $$327^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$ then energy emitted per second becomes
en.explanation:
$$\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{e} \sigma \cdot \mathrm{A}\left(\mathrm{T}^4-\mathrm{T}_0^4\right) \text { and } \mathrm{A}=\ell \mathrm{b}$$

When $$\ell$$ and $$b$$ change to $$\frac{\ell}{3}$$ and $$\frac{b}{3}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & A^{\prime}=\frac{A}{9} \\ & \frac{E^{\prime}}{E}=\frac{A^{\prime}}{A} \frac{(327+273)^4}{(27+273)^4} ; \quad \frac{E^{\prime}}{E}=\frac{1}{9}\left(\frac{600}{300}\right)^4 \\ & \therefore E^{\prime}=\frac{1}{9} \times(2)^4 \times E \quad \Rightarrow E^{\prime}=\frac{16 E}{9} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A closed organ pipe of length '$$\mathrm{L}_c$$' and an open organ pipe of length '$$\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{o}}$$' contain different gases of densities '$$\rho_1$$' and '$$\rho_2$$' respectively. The compressibility of the gases is the same in both the pipes. The gases are vibrating in their first overtone with the same frequency. What is the length of open organ pipe?
en.explanation:
For open organ pipe :

Fundamental frequency $$n=\frac{V}{2 L_o}$$

First overtone $$\mathrm{n}_1=2 \mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{o}}}$$

For closed organ pipe

Fundamental frequency $$\mathrm{n}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{V}^{\prime}}{4 \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{c}}}$$

First overtone $$n_1^{\prime}=3 n^{\prime}=\frac{3 V^{\prime}}{4 L_c}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{n}_1 & =\mathrm{n}_1^{\prime} \quad \therefore \frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{o}}}=\frac{3 \mathrm{~V}^{\prime}}{4 \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{c}}} \\ \therefore \frac{\mathrm{L}_0}{\mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{c}}} & =\frac{4}{3} \frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{V}^{\prime}} \quad \text{.......(1)}\\ \mathrm{V} & =\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\rho_2}}, \mathrm{~V}^{\prime}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\rho_{\mathrm{l}}}} \end{aligned}$$

where $$\mathrm{k}$$ is the adiabatic bulk modulus, which is reciprocal of compressibility.

$$\therefore \frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{V}^{\prime}}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}}$$

Putting this value in Eq.(1)

$$\frac{\mathrm{L}_0}{\mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{c}}}=\frac{4}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{\rho}_1}{\rho_2}}$$

en.content: The moment of inertia of a circular disc of radius $$2 \mathrm{~m}$$ and mass $$1 \mathrm{~kg}$$ about an axis XY passing through its centre of mass and perpendicular to the plane of the disc is $$2 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^2$$. The moment of inertia about an axis parallel to the axis $$\mathrm{XY}$$ and passing through the edge of the disc is
A progressive wave of frequency 50 Hz is travelling with velocity 350 m/s through a medium. The change in phase at a given time interval of 0.01 second is
en.explanation:

If $$\mathrm{T}$$ is the period and phase difference is $$\phi$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \text { then, } \frac{\mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{\phi}{2 \pi} \\ & \therefore \phi=2 \pi \frac{\mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{T}}=2 \pi \mathrm{nt} \\ & \therefore \phi=2 \pi \times 50 \times 0.01=\pi \mathrm{~rad} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A simple harmonic progressive wave is given by $$Y=Y_0 \sin 2 \pi\left(n t-\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)$$. If the wave velocity is $$\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{\text {th }}$$ the maximum particle velocity then the wavelength is

Wave velocity $$=n \lambda$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{2 \pi n Y_0}{8}=n \lambda \\ & \therefore \lambda=\frac{\pi Y_0}{4} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: In a meter bridge experiment, the balance point is obtained at length $$\ell_1 \mathrm{~cm}$$ from left end when resistances in the left gap and right gap are $$5 \Omega$$ and $$R \Omega$$ respectively. When the resistance $$R$$ is shunted with equal resistance, the new balance point is at $$1.6 \ell_1$$. The resitance $$R$$ in ohm is
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{5}{R}=\frac{\ell_1}{100 \ell_1} \quad \text{.......(1)}\\ & \frac{5 \times 2}{R}=\frac{1.6 \ell_1}{100-1.6 \ell} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{5}{R}=\frac{0.8 \ell_1}{100-1.6 \ell_1} \quad \text{.......(2)} \end{aligned}$$

Equating (1) and (2) and solving we get $$\ell_1=25 \mathrm{~cm}$$ Putting this in Eq.(1), we get $$\mathrm{R}=15 \Omega$$

en.content: In the graphical representation of e.m.f. '$$\mathrm{e}$$' and current '$$\mathrm{i}$$' versus '$$\omega \mathrm{t}$$' for an a.c. circuit, both emf and current reach zero, minimum and maximum value at the same time. The circuit element connected to the source will be

en.content: The moment of inertia of a body about a given axis is $$1.2 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$$. Initially the body is at rest. In order to produce rotational kinetic energy of $$1500 \mathrm{~J}$$, an angular acceleration of $$25 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2$$ must be applied about an axis for a time duration of
en.explanation: $$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}=1.2 \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{m}^2, \quad \text { K.E. }=1500 \mathrm{~J}, \alpha=25 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2 \\ & \text { K.E. }=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2 \\ & \therefore 1500=\frac{1}{2} \times 1.2 \times \omega^2 \\ & \therefore \omega^2=\frac{2 \times 1500}{1.2}=2500 \quad \therefore \omega=50 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \quad \omega=\omega_0+\alpha \mathrm{t} \\ & \therefore 50=0+25 \mathrm{t}=25 \mathrm{t} \quad \therefore \mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: An alternating voltge is represented by $$\mathrm{V}=80 \sin (100 \pi \mathrm{t}) \cos (100 \pi \mathrm{t})$$ volt. The peak voltage is
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} & \sin 2 \theta=2 \sin \theta \cdot \cos \theta \\ & \begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad \sin \theta \cos \theta=\frac{\sin 2 \theta}{2} \\ & \mathrm{~V}=80 \sin (100 \pi \mathrm{t}) \cos (100 \pi \mathrm{t}) \\ &=\frac{80 \sin 200 \pi \mathrm{t}}{2}=40 \sin 200 \pi \mathrm{t} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

Amplitude or the peak value of the voltage $$=40 \mathrm{~V}$$

en.content: When the value of acceleration due to gravity '$$g$$' becomes $$\frac{g}{3}$$ above surface of height '$$h$$' then relation between '$$h$$' and '$$R$$' is ( $$\mathrm{R}=$$ radius of earth)
en.explanation: $$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\mathrm{g} \frac{\mathrm{R}^2}{(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})^2} \quad \mathrm{~g}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{g}}{3} \\ & \therefore \frac{1}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{R}^2}{(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})^2} \quad \therefore \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}} \\ & \therefore \sqrt{3} \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{h}=(\sqrt{3}-1) \mathrm{R}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: In biprism experiment, 21 fringes are observed in a given region using light of wavelength 4800 $$\mathop A\limits^o $$. If light of wavelength 5600 $$\mathop A\limits^o $$ is used, the number of fringes in the same region will be

en.content: A wire of length '$$L$$'; having resistance '$$R$$' falls from a height '$$\ell$$' in earth's horizontal magnetic field '$$B$$'. The current through the wire is ( $$\mathrm{g}=$$ acceleration due to gravity)
en.explanation:
If the wire falls through a height $$h$$, the velocity acquired by it is $$\mathrm{v}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g} \ell}$$

The emf induced in the wire

$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{e}=\mathrm{BLv}=\mathrm{BL} \sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g} \ell} \\ \therefore \text { Current } \mathrm{I} & =\frac{\mathrm{e}}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{\mathrm{BL} \sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g} \ell}}{\mathrm{R}} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Two wires '$$\mathrm{A}$$' and '$$\mathrm{B}$$' of equal length are connected in left and right gap respectively of meter bridge, null point is obtained at $$40 \mathrm{~cm}$$, from the left end. Diameters of the wires '$$A$$' and '$$B$$' are in the ratio $$3: 1$$ respectively, the ratio of specific resistance of 'A' to that of 'B' is
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{R_A}{R_B}=\frac{40}{60}=\frac{2}{3} \\ & R=\rho \cdot \frac{\ell}{A}=\rho \cdot \frac{\ell}{\pi r^2} \end{aligned}$$

Length of the wires are same.

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{A}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{B}}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right)^2 \\ & \therefore \frac{2}{3}=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{A}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{B}}}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{A}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{B}}} \cdot \frac{1}{9} \\ & \therefore \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{A}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{B}}}=6 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A glass cube of length $$24 \mathrm{~cm}$$ has a small air bubble trapped inside. When viewed normally from one face it is $$10 \mathrm{~cm}$$ below the surface. When viewed normally from the opposite face, its apparent distance is $$6 \mathrm{~cm}$$. The refractive index of glass is
en.explanation:
Let $$x$$ be the real depth when the apparent depth is $$10 \mathrm{~cm}$$.

$$\therefore \mu=\frac{x}{10}$$

Let $$\mathrm{y}$$ be the real depth when the apparent depth is $$6 \mathrm{~cm}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mu=\frac{y}{6} \\ & \therefore \frac{x}{10}=\frac{y}{6} \quad \therefore x=\frac{5}{3} y \end{aligned}$$

Also $$x+y=24$$

$$\therefore \frac{5}{3} y+y=24 \quad \therefore \frac{8}{3} y=24$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore y & =9 \mathrm{~cm} \\ \mu & =\frac{y}{6}=\frac{9}{6}=1.5 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: What is susceptibility of a medium, if its relative permeability is 0.85?
en.explanation:
Relative permeability $$\mu_r=1+\chi$$

$$\therefore \chi=\mu_r-1=0.85-1=-0.15$$

en.content: In fundamental mode, the time required for the sound wave to reach upto the closed end of pipe filled with air is $$t$$ second. The frequency of vibration of air column is
en.explanation:
In fundamental mode the length of the closed tube is $$\frac{\lambda}{4}$$

Time required to travel a distance $$\frac{\lambda}{4}$$ is t.

Hence time required to travel a distance $$\lambda$$ will be $$4 \mathrm{t}$$.

$$\therefore$$ Time period $$\mathrm{T}=4 \mathrm{t}$$;

Frequency $$\mathrm{n}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{~T}}=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{t}}=\frac{0.25}{\mathrm{t}}$$

en.content: A particle of mass '$$m$$' is kept at rest at a height $$3 R$$ from the surface of earth, where '$$R$$' is radius of earth and '$$M$$' is the mass of earth. The minimum speed with which it should be projected, so that it does not return back is ( $$g=$$ acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface)
en.explanation:
For the particle to escape from earth's gravitational field, it should be given kinetic energy equal to its binding energy.

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2=\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{4 \mathrm{R}} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{V}=\left[\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{2 \mathrm{R}}\right]^{1 / 2} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: '$$\mathrm{F}$$' is the force between the two identical charged particles placed at a distance '$$\mathrm{Y}$$' from each other. If the distance between the charges is reduced to half the previous distance then force between them becomes
en.explanation: $$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{F}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{q}^2}{\mathrm{r}^2} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{F}_2}{\mathrm{~F}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^2=(2)^2=4 \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{F}_2=4 \mathrm{~F}_1\end{aligned}$$

en.content: A coil of radius '$$\mathrm{r}$$' is placed on another coil (whose radius is '$$\mathrm{R}$$' and current through it is changing) so that their centres coincide. ( $$R > r$$ ). If both coplanar, then the mutual inductance between them is proportional to
en.explanation:
Magnetic field at the centre $$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{R}$$

$$\phi=$$ Magnetic flux passing through the smaller coil $$=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{~B}$$

$$\therefore \phi=\pi r^2 \times \frac{\mu_0 I}{R}$$

$$\therefore M=\frac{\phi}{I}=\frac{\mu \pi r^2}{R} \quad \therefore M \propto \frac{r^2}{R}$$

en.content: '$$\lambda_1$$' is the wavelength of series limit of Lyman series, '$$\lambda_2$$' is the wavelength of the first line line of Lyman series and '$$\lambda_3$$' is the series limit of the Balmer series. Then the relation between $$\lambda_1, \lambda_2$$ and $$\lambda_3$$ is
en.explanation:
Series limit of Lyman series is given by

$$\frac{1}{\lambda_1}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=\mathrm{R}$$

Series limit of Balmer series is given by

$$\frac{1}{\lambda_3}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{4}$$

First line of Lyman series is given by

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\lambda_2}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\mathrm{R}-\frac{\mathrm{R}}{4}=\frac{1}{\lambda_1}-\frac{1}{\lambda_3} \\ \therefore & \frac{1}{\lambda_1}-\frac{1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{1}{\lambda_3} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The velocity of a small ball of mass '$$M$$' and density '$$\mathrm{d}_1$$' when dropped in a container filled with glycerine becomes constant after some time. If the density of glycerine is '$$\mathrm{d}_2$$', the viscous force acting on the ball is ( $$\mathrm{g}=$$ acceleration due to gravity)
en.explanation:
Since the velocity is constant, the net force acting on the ball is zero. Forces acting are Since the veloll $$=\mathrm{Mg}$$ (downwards)

$$\begin{aligned} \text { Weight of } & =\text { weight of water displaced } \\ & =(\text { volume of water }) \times(\text { density of water }) \times g \\ & =(\text { volume of ball }) \times(\text { density of water }) \times g \end{aligned}$$

$$=\frac{M}{d_1} \times d_2 \times g=M g \frac{d_2}{d_1}$$ (upwards)

$$F=$$ viscous force (upwards)

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore F+M g \frac{d_2}{d_1}=M g \\ & \therefore F=M g\left(1-\frac{d_2}{d_1}\right) \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A sphere of mass 25 gram is placed on a vertical spring. It is compressed by $$0.2 \mathrm{~m}$$ using a force $$5 \mathrm{~N}$$. When the spring is released, the sphere will reach a height of $$\left(\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$$ $$2 \mathrm{~m}$$
en.explanation:
Gravitational potential energy gained by the ball = Elastic potential energy in the spring

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{mgh} & =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{Fx} \\ \therefore \quad \mathrm{h} & =\frac{\mathrm{Fx}}{2 \mathrm{mg}} \\ & =\frac{5 \times 0.2}{2 \times 25 \times 10^{-3} \times 10} \\ & =2 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A bomb is dropped by an aeroplane flying horizontally with a velocity $$200 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{hr}$$ and at a height of $$980 \mathrm{~m}$$. At the time of dropping a bomb, the distance of the aeroplane from the target on the ground to hit directly is $$\left(g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$$
en.explanation:
The plane is flying horizontally. Hence initial vertical component of the velocity is zero. If it reaches the ground in time $$t$$, then

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{h} & =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{gt}^2 \quad \therefore \mathrm{t}^2=\frac{2 \mathrm{~h}}{\mathrm{~g}}=\frac{2 \times 980}{9.8}=200 \\ \therefore \mathrm{t} & =10 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~s} \end{aligned}$$

The horizontal component of the velocity is

$$\mathrm{V}=200 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{hr}=200 \times \frac{5}{18}=\frac{1000}{18} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$$

The horizontal distance to be covered is

$$d=V t=\frac{1000}{18} \times 10 \sqrt{2}=\frac{10^4}{9 \sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~m}$$

en.content: A series combination of resistor 'R' and capacitor 'C' is connected to an a.c. source of angular frequency '$$\omega$$'. Keeping the voltage same, if the frequency is changed to $$\frac{\omega}{3}$$ the current becomes half of the original current. Then the ratio of capacitive reactance and resistance at the former frequency is
en.explanation:
Initial current $$\mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{z}}$$, Final current $$\mathrm{I}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{z}}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2}=\frac{\mathrm{I}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\mathrm{z}}{\mathrm{z}^{\prime}} \quad \therefore \frac{\mathrm{z}}{\mathrm{z}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{z}^2}{\mathrm{z}^{\prime 2}}=\frac{1}{4} \quad \therefore \frac{\mathrm{R}^2+\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}^2}{\mathrm{R}^2+\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\prime 2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ & \therefore 4 \mathrm{R}^2+4 \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}^2=\mathrm{R}^2+\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\prime 2} \\ & \therefore 3 \mathrm{R}^2=\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\prime 2}-4 \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}^2 \quad \text{......(1)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{1}{\omega C}, \mathrm{X}^{\prime}=\frac{3}{\omega C} \quad \therefore \mathrm{X}^{\prime}=3 \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}$$

Putting this value of $$X^{\prime}$$ in (1) we get

$$3 R^2=9 X_c^2-4 X_c^2=5 X_c^2$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}^2}{\mathrm{R}^2}=\frac{3}{5}=0.6 \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{R}}=\sqrt{0.6} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A double slit experiment is immersed in water of refractive index 1.33. The slit separationis 1 $$\mathrm{mm}$$ and the distance between slit and screen is $$1.33 \mathrm{~m}$$. The slits are illuminated by a light of wavelength $$6300\,\mathop A\limits^o $$. The fringewidth is
en.explanation: $$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{d}=1 \mathrm{~mm}=10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}, \mathrm{D}=1.33 \mathrm{~m} \\ & \lambda=6300 \mathop A\limits^o=6.3 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m} \\ & \lambda_w=\text { wavelength in water }=\frac{6.3 \times 10^{-7}}{1.33} \mathrm{~m} \\ & \text { Fringe width } \mathrm{X}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{w}} \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{6.3 \times 10^{-7} \times 1.33}{1.33 \times 10^{-3}}=6.3 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: Two small drops of mercury each of radius '$$R$$' coalesce to form a large single drop. The ratio of the total surface energies before and after the change is
en.explanation:
Total surface energy before coalesce

$$\mathrm{E}_1=2\left(4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2\right) \mathrm{T}$$

But $$\frac{4}{3} \pi R^2 \times 2=\frac{4}{3} \pi R^{\prime 3}$$

Total surface energy after coalesce

$$\begin{aligned} & E_2=4 \pi R^{\prime 2} T=4 \pi 2^{2 / 3} R^2 T \\ & \therefore \frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{2\left(4 \pi R^2\right) T}{4 \pi 2^{2 / 3} R^2 T}=2^{1-\frac{2}{3}}=2^{1 / 3} \end{aligned}$$

en.explanation: The kinetic energy of the photo electrons and hence the stopping potential does not depend on the intensity of light.

en.content: A particle executes linear S.H.M. The mean position of oscillation is at the principal axis of a convex lens of focal length $$8 \mathrm{~cm}$$. the mean position of oscillation is at 14 cm from the lens with amplitude 1 cm. The amplitude of oscillating image of the particle is nearly
en.explanation:
$$\mathrm{f}=8 \mathrm{~cm}$$, when the particle is at mean position, $$\mathrm{u}=-14 \mathrm{~cm}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\mathrm{v}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{u}}=\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{14}=\frac{3}{56} \\ & \therefore \quad v=\frac{56}{3} \quad \approx 19 \mathrm{~cm} \\ \end{aligned}$$

When the particle is at one of the extreme positions its distance from the lens is $$14+1=15 \mathrm{~cm}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{u}=-15 \mathrm{~cm} \\ & \text { Again, } \frac{1}{\mathrm{v}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{u}}=\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{15}=\frac{7}{120} \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{v}=\frac{120}{7} \quad \approx 17 \mathrm{~cm} \end{aligned}$$

Amplitude of the image $$=19-17=2 \mathrm{~cm}$$
